name: Classical rotor burst limit v = sqrt(sigma/rho), independent of radius

source.located: Classical engineering mechanics, no single arXiv source: thin-ring hoop balance sigma = rho v^2 (textbook elasticity, e.g. Timoshenko & Goodier, Theory of Elasticity, rotating discs; Stodola's constant-strength disc; Genta, Kinetic Energy Storage 1985, shape factor K). Candidate arXiv restatement: arXiv:2103.05224 ('A review of flywheel energy storage systems: state of the art and opportunities').

published_statement: Not quoted at source (NAMED-NOT-READ). The classical content, as re-derived here: a thin rim (all mass at radius R, uniaxial hoop stress) spinning at tip speed v = omega R carries hoop stress sigma_h = rho v^2, so it fails when v exceeds sqrt(sigma/rho); the limit contains no R. Search-summary paraphrase of arXiv:2103.05224: 'If all the mass of a rotor is concentrated at the rim, the maximum tip speed is (sigma/rho)^(1/2)' -- note the rim hypothesis is in the sentence itself.
published_hypotheses: all mass concentrated at the rim (thin rim, radial thickness << R) -- stated in the restated sentence itself
uniaxial hoop stress; radial and axial stresses neglected
linear elastic, quasi-static rotation (no vibration, no creep/fatigue), non-relativistic
sigma is the strength of the rim material in the hoop direction

for other geometries the classical treatment gives a different factor: uniform disc v_max = sqrt(8 sigma/((3+nu) rho)); constant-strength (Stodola/Laval) disc has K = 1 and no tip-speed ceiling from the same argument
hypothesis_drift: DROPPED at warpfolder.py:117-118: 'A rotor asked to exceed sqrt(sigma/rho) does not spin; it disassembles.' states the thin-rim limit as universal over rotors. Re-derived here: a uniform solid disc reaches sqrt(8/(3+nu)) = 1.557 sqrt(sigma/rho) (nu = 0.3), and a constant-stress (Stodola) disc h = h0 exp(-rho omega^2 r^2/2 sigma) closed by a thin rim of section A = R h0 sigma e^{-rho v^2/2 sigma}/(rho v^2 - (1-nu) sigma) is in equilibrium and compatible at ANY v > sqrt((1-nu) sigma/rho). The sentence is a thin-rim statement, not a theorem about all rotors.

DROPPED at warpfolder.py:329 docstring 'The classical rotor limit sqrt(sigma/rho), independent of radius': no geometry named. Compare the tree's own earlier sites which KEEP it: warpdrive.py:235 'Burst surface speed of a thin spinning cylinder: hoop stress = rho v^2' and ENGINE-ASSESSMENT.md:196 'A thin spinning cylinder bursts when hoop stress reaches the material limit'.
KEPT, correctly: 'independent of radius' (warpfolder.py:329) holds at fixed shape for every geometry checked (rim, solid disc, bored disc at fixed a/R, Stodola) -- stress scales as rho v^2.

SUBSTITUTED at warpfolder.py:225: sigma for T1000 is the bare-fibre tensile strength 6.4 GPa and rho the fibre density 1800; a rotor is a composite. Rule-of-mixtures UPPER bound (Vf 0.55-0.65, resin 1200 kg/m3) gives v_rim <= 1517-1618 m/s and ratio >= 4.95-5.28x, so the substitution is in the rotor's FAVOUR -- it does not flatter the refusal. The owner's comment at warpfolder.py:222-223 says sigma/rho 'are NOT from the folder ... so they carry their own status', but the status word on the MATERIALS row is ORDER only.

NOT MODELLED (named, not computed): radial/transverse failure of thick composite rims (transverse strength of order tens of MPa), which lowers the composite limit further; fatigue and safety factor; the diameter-vs-radius reading of 'Flywheel Rotor 1.8 m' (warpfolder.py:218 reads it as a diameter -- the radius reading doubles v and both ratios).

rederivation.outcome: ALL PASS (exit 0). (1) Thin rim: sigma_h = rho v^2, v_max = sqrt(sigma/rho), no R, K = 1/2. (2) Uniform solid disc from the Lame equation: peak sigma = (3+nu)/8 rho omega^2 R^2 at the centre, v_max = 2 sqrt(2)/sqrt(3+nu) sqrt(sigma/rho) = 1.557x at nu = 0.3, K = 2/(3+nu) = 0.606. (3) Pinhole bore: (3+nu)/4 rho omega^2 R^2, v_max = 1.101x; a -> R recovers the thin rim. (4) Stodola disc satisfies equilibrium and compatibility for every omega; K -> 1 as R -> infinity (matches the restated 'Laval disc K = 1'); closing rim section A > 0 for any v > sqrt((1-nu) sigma/rho) -- a formal counterexample to the universal sentence at warpfolder.py:117-118. (5) Tree numbers: tip 8011.06 m/s; burst 1885.6 and 411.9 m/s; ratios 4.2485 and 19.4470, rounding to the pinned [4.2, 19.4]; warpfolder.burst_speed_m_s agrees to 1e-9. (6) Every non-profiled geometry leaves both materials over the limit (T1000 2.73-4.25x, BeCu 12.49-19.45x). The Stodola escape needs h(R)/h(0) = 1.2e-4 for T1000 treated as an isotropic material with fibre sigma/rho (no such material exists) and 7.5e-83 for BeCu (physically empty).

lacked_data: M's hypothesis tested: did the originators lack data that changes this? No. The result is a closed-form consequence of Newtonian force balance and linear elasticity; it takes no empirical input except the material's sigma and rho, which enter only as the ratio sigma/rho. What the classical authors lacked were modern materials (carbon fibre, maraging steels); those raise sigma/rho but do not touch the formula. Evidence against a data move changing THIS conclusion: the demanded 8011 m/s needs sigma/rho raised 18x (T1000, rim) / 7.4x (T1000, uniform disc) / 378x (BeCu, rim); replacing the bare-fibre T1000 figure with any composite value moves the ratio UP (>= 4.95x); the BeCu datasheet spread moves it only within 18.2-21.1x. Evidence FOR an incompleteness, found here and not in M's favour or against it: the limit is incomplete as the tree words it -- it is a thin-rim result, and the constant-stress disc formally escapes it -- but this is a hypothesis the tree drops, not missing data, and it does not rescue the rotor with the named materials.
grade_evidence: The formula v = sqrt(sigma/rho), and its independence of radius, are re-derived exactly for the thin rim (sympy, script exit 0), and the tree's numbers (8011.06 m/s; 4.2x, 19.4x) are reproduced to four figures. But the tree uses it on a larger class than it holds on: warpfolder.py:117-118 says any rotor asked to exceed sqrt(sigma/rho) disassembles, whereas a uniform disc reaches 1.557x and a Stodola constant-stress disc with a thin closing rim is in equilibrium at any tip speed (shown symbolically). The dependent conclusion ROTOR_IS_WITHIN_MATERIAL_LIMITS = False (warpfolder.py:247, :569-570) survives on every geometry checked -- ratios 2.73-4.25x (T1000) and 12.49-19.45x (BeCu) -- and the Stodola escape needs a tip-to-hub thickness ratio of 1.2e-4 with a fictitious isotropic T1000 and 7.5e-83 with BeCu; the bare-fibre T1000 figure is favourable to the rotor, not to the refusal. So: the burst limit STANDS for the thin rim, is NARROWED as a universal rotor limit, and the refusal's factors are geometry-dependent ('over by 4.2x' is the thin-rim factor; the uniform-disc factor is 2.7x). Source NOT READ at arXiv this stage (quota/egress); the grade rests on the rederivation, not on a reading.
what_would_change_the_grade: To STANDS: the owner restores the thin-rim (or 'non-profiled geometry') hypothesis at warpfolder.py:117-118 and :329, as warpdrive.py:235 and ENGINE-ASSESSMENT.md:196 already do. To WRONG for the dependent refusal: a realisable profiled rotor of either named material shown to hold 8011 m/s (none exists on the numbers here). A reading of arXiv:2103.05224 or Genta 1985 at source would upgrade read_status but cannot move the grade unless it states a different formula, which the derivation here makes implausible.
